papers.research_question: Does the approach of semantic feature extraction via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising route for AI safety, and how generalizable are the claims about interpretable features and feature steering made by Anthropic?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that while sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based feature extraction and steering can produce compelling demonstrations, the methods exhibit substantial fragility and context-dependence, falling short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE-based interpretability methods are not reliable enough for safety-critical applications, suggesting a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering is fragile, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context.
There exist non-standard activation behaviors (e.g., high activation density, disproportionate activation on the beginning-of-text token) that are not captured by automated feature interpretations.
It is difficult to distinguish thematically similar features from one another, even within the same layer.
Automated interpretations of features (labels) often do not align with the features' activation patterns across text samples or their effects when used for model steering.
SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases but current methods often lack systematic reliability.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to one publicly available model (Llama 3.1-8B) and a specific set of pre-trained SAEs (Llama Scope).
The study does not have internal access to Anthropic's proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.0 Sonnet) and relies on the assumption of a weak form of universality.
future_direction: Future work should focus on reliable prediction and control of model output, rather than just interpretability of internal representations.
More research is needed to understand the conditions under which interpretable features emerge and to verify that they function computationally in ways analogous to human concepts.
papers.abstract: Recent work by Anthropic on Mechanistic interpretability claims to understand and control Large Language Models by extracting human-interpretable features from their neural activation patterns using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If successful, this approach offers one of the most promising routes for human oversight in AI safety. We conduct an initial stress-test of these claims by replicating their main results with open-source SAEs for Llama 3.1. While we successfully reproduce basic feature extraction and steering capabilities, our investigation suggests that major caution is warranted regarding the generalizability of these claims. We find that feature steering exhibits substantial fragility, with sensitivity to layer selection, steering magnitude, and context. We observe non-standard activation behavior and demonstrate the difficulty to distinguish thematically similar features from one another. While SAE-based interpretability produces compelling demonstrations in selected cases, current methods often fall short of the systematic reliability required for safety-critical applications. This suggests a necessary shift in focus from prioritizing interpretability of internal representations toward reliable prediction and control of model output. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of what mechanistic interpretability has achieved and highlights fundamental challenges for AI safety that remain unresolved.

papers.title: Automating Steering for Safe Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the safety of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be improved during inference without fine-tuning, by automatically identifying safety-relevant internal layers and adaptively steering generation to refuse harmful inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AutoSteer, a modular and adaptive inference-time intervention framework that automatically identifies safety-relevant layers via a Safety Awareness Score (SAS), uses a lightweight safety prober to detect toxicity, and conditionally activates a refusal head to steer generation, significantly improving MLLM safety without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: AutoSteer offers a practical, interpretable, and effective inference-time framework for enhancing MLLM safety across multimodal threats while preserving general capabilities, providing a scalable solution for safer deployment.
papers.key_findings:
AutoSteer significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) for textual, visual, and cross-modal threats on LLaVA-OV and Chameleon models.
The framework preserves general task performance (utility) while enhancing safety, avoiding the utility degradation common in global steering methods.
The Safety Awareness Score (SAS) effectively identifies internal layers with the clearest safety-relevant distinctions, validated by probing accuracy and cosine similarity analysis.
Steering intensity (ϵ) has a nonlinear effect on ASR, with diminishing returns at higher values, and can cause unintended output drift or instability if applied uniformly.
The safety prober's outputs are highly polarized, limiting its effectiveness for fine-grained, continuous toxicity control.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of the safety prober depends on the quality and diversity of its training data and is constrained by the underlying MLLM's internal safety awareness.
The method involves separate training of the safety prober and refusal head, adding complexity and requiring model-specific calibration.
Experiments are conducted on a limited number of MLLMs, so generalizability to broader architectures, especially larger models, is not fully guaranteed.
future_direction: Validate AutoSteer across a broader range of MLLMs, such as larger and newer architectures.
Improve the safety prober's robustness via training with diverse and adversarial data.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has unlocked powerful cross-modal reasoning abilities, but also raised new safety concerns, particularly when faced with adversarial multimodal inputs. To improve the safety of MLLMs during inference, we introduce a modular and adaptive inference-time intervention technology, AutoSteer, without requiring any fine-tuning of the underlying model. AutoSteer incorporates three core components: (1) a novel Safety Awareness Score (SAS) that automatically identifies the most safety-relevant distinctions among the model's internal layers; (2) an adaptive safety prober trained to estimate the likelihood of toxic outputs from intermediate representations; and (3) a lightweight Refusal Head that selectively intervenes to modulate generation when safety risks are detected. Experiments on LLaVA-OV and Chameleon across diverse safety-critical benchmarks demonstrate that AutoSteer significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) for textual, visual, and cross-modal threats, while maintaining general abilities. These findings position AutoSteer as a practical, interpretable, and effective framework for safer deployment of multimodal AI systems.

papers.title: SOM Directions are Better than One: Multi-Directional Refusal Suppression in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is refusal behavior in language models better represented by a single linear direction or by a low-dimensional manifold of multiple directions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a multi-directional approach using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to model refusal as a manifold, showing that ablating multiple directions is more effective for refusal suppression than ablating a single direction.
papers.conclusion: Modeling refusal as a manifold spanned by multiple, closely related directions provides a more faithful and effective view of safety-related behaviors in LLMs than the single-direction perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating multiple refusal directions identified by SOMs (MD) significantly outperforms the single-direction baseline (SD) and other jailbreak algorithms (GCG, SAA) in terms of Attack Success Rate (ASR).
Ablating multiple directions compresses the variance of harmful prompt representations and shifts them closer to harmless representations in the model's activation space.
The multiple directions extracted by SOMs are closely related (non-orthogonal), suggesting refusal is encoded as a manifold rather than a set of orthogonal components.
The method is effective even against a model with a defense mechanism (Mistral-7B-RR).
The effectiveness of refusal suppression generally increases with the number of ablated directions (k).
papers.limitation:
The Bayesian Optimization search for the best combination of directions can require a high number of trials as the search space grows, impacting scalability and speed.
The method computes directions at a single layer and applies ablation uniformly across all layers, potentially missing layer-specific variations in refusal encoding.
future_direction: Explore more efficient or structured search strategies, gradient-based optimization, or pruning algorithms to improve the scalability of the direction search.
Investigate layer-specific directions and ablation strategies to better capture refusal encoding across different layers.
Investigate the effectiveness of training separate SOMs for harmless prompts instead of using a single centroid.
papers.abstract: Refusal refers to the functional behavior enabling safety-aligned language models to reject harmful or unethical prompts. Following the growing scientific interest in mechanistic interpretability, recent work encoded refusal behavior as a single direction in the model's latent space; e.g., computed as the difference between the centroids of harmful and harmless prompt representations. However, emerging evidence suggests that concepts in LLMs often appear to be encoded as a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional latent space. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method leveraging Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to extract multiple refusal directions. To this end, we first prove that SOMs generalize the prior work's difference-in-means technique. We then train SOMs on harmful prompt representations to identify multiple neurons. By subtracting the centroid of harmless representations from each neuron, we derive a set of multiple directions expressing the refusal concept. We validate our method on an extensive experimental setup, demonstrating that ablating multiple directions from models' internals outperforms not only the single-direction baseline but also specialized jailbreak algorithms, leading to an effective suppression of refusal. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the mechanistic implications of our approach.

papers.title: Extracting Visual Facts from Intermediate Layers for Mitigating Hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does prior knowledge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) suppress visual factual knowledge at the intermediate layer stage, and how can this be leveraged to mitigate object hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EV A, a training-free decoding method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with rich visual factual knowledge, contrasts their output distributions from multimodal and text-only inputs to extract this knowledge, and integrates it into the final layer to correct hallucinatory outputs.
papers.conclusion: EV A, a train-free decoding method that revises final outputs by extracting visual factual knowledge from intermediate layers, significantly reduces the incidence of hallucinations in MLLMs, highlighting its effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Visual factual knowledge and the Jensen-Shannon divergence between intermediate-layer original/prior probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends.
The intermediate layer with the maximum JS divergence contains richer visual factual knowledge.
EV A significantly reduces hallucination rates on benchmarks (POPE, MME, CHAIR) compared to baseline methods like DoLa, VCD, OPERA, and DeCo.
EV A is model-agnostic and seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies (greedy search, nucleus sampling, beam search).
EV A's mechanism of subtracting LLM priors can lead to a decline in the model's original recognition capabilities on some tasks.
papers.limitation: Due to GPU cost constraints, experiments are exclusively conducted on a limited set of MLLMs, without exploring additional models or those with larger parameter scales.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have made significant strides by combining visual recognition and language understanding to generate content that is both coherent and contextually accurate. However, MLLMs continue to struggle with object hallucinations, where models produce seemingly plausible but factually incorrect outputs, including objects that do not exist in the image. Recent work has revealed that the prior knowledge in MLLMs significantly suppresses visual information in deep layers, causing hallucinatory outputs. However, how these priors suppress visual information at the intermediate layer stage in MLLMs remains unclear. We observe that visual factual knowledge and the differences between intermediate-layer prior/original probability distributions show similar evolutionary trends in intermediate layers. Motivated by this, we introduce Decoding by Extracting Visual Facts (EVA), a simple, training-free method that dynamically selects intermediate layers with the most significant visual factual information. By contrasting the output distributions of the selected layer derived from the original input and pure-text input, EVA extracts visual factual knowledge and proportionally incorporates it into the final layer to correct the output logits. Importantly, EVA is model-agnostic, seamlessly integrates with various classic decoding strategies, and is applicable across different MLLMs. We validate EVA on widely-used benchmarks, and the results show that it significantly reduces hallucination rates compared to baseline methods, underscoring its effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: Can the safety alignment of instruction-tuned Large Language Models be bypassed by injecting trojan steering vectors into their activation layers at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Trojan Activation Attack (TA2), a method that injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs to break their safety alignment efficiently and with high stealth at inference time.
papers.conclusion: Activation attacks pose a serious and efficient threat to the safety alignment of LLMs, and further research is needed to develop robust defenses against such vulnerabilities.
papers.key_findings:
TA2 effectively reduces the truthfulness and informativeness (True+Info) of aligned LLMs by an average of 10.68%.
TA2 significantly increases toxic generation (avg. +58.11%) and decreases refusal rates (avg. -59.18%) for toxicity prompts.
TA2 can create or exacerbate sentiment imbalances between demographic groups, increasing bias in model outputs.
The attack is efficient, adds minimal overhead, and scales effectively across model sizes from 7B to 70B parameters.
TA2 demonstrates higher effectiveness on Vicuna-V1.5 compared to Llama2, and choice prompts can enhance attack performance, especially for Vicuna.
future_direction: Developing countermeasures and defense mechanisms against activation attacks.
Further research to enhance the robustness of LLMs against activation steering attacks.
papers.abstract: To ensure AI safety, instruction-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are specifically trained to ensure alignment, which refers to making models behave in accordance with human intentions. While these models have demonstrated commendable results on various safety benchmarks, the vulnerability of their safety alignment has not been extensively studied. This is particularly troubling given the potential harm that LLMs can inflict. Existing attack methods on LLMs often rely on poisoned training data or the injection of malicious prompts. These approaches compromise the stealthiness and generalizability of the attacks, making them susceptible to detection. Additionally, these models often demand substantial computational resources for implementation, making them less practical for real-world applications. In this work, we study a different attack scenario, called Trojan Activation Attack (TA^2), which injects trojan steering vectors into the activation layers of LLMs. These malicious steering vectors can be triggered at inference time to steer the models toward attacker-desired behaviors by manipulating their activations. Our experiment results on four primary alignment tasks show that TA^2 is highly effective and adds little or no overhead to attack efficiency. Additionally, we discuss potential countermeasures against such activation attacks.

papers.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically identify effective trigger instructions for reflection, and do these instructions correspond to latent directions in the model's hidden space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using activation steering to identify latent directions of reflection in LLMs, enabling systematic discovery of reflection-inducing instructions and control over reflective behavior, with the finding that suppressing reflection is easier than enhancing it.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that reflection corresponds to consistent activation patterns, paving the way for future interpretability work, and highlight a dual-use concern where steering can enhance reflection as a defense mechanism but also be exploited to inhibit reflection for jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Reflection levels (no, intrinsic, triggered) show clear stratification in model accuracy.
Steering vectors can discover new reflection-inducing instructions beyond known ones.
Reflection can be enhanced or inhibited via activation interventions at inference time.
Suppressing reflection is easier than inducing it.
Latent directions of reflection are more faithfully captured by steering vectors than by surface-level embedding similarity.
papers.limitation:
The method provides a broad overview of reflection in activations but does not drill down into specific components like attention heads or MLP neurons.
Experiments are limited to two small-sized models (Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT) and two datasets.
Theoretical understanding is limited; accuracy does not vary linearly with latent directions, requiring deeper treatment.
future_direction: Applying fine-grained approaches like activation patching, causal tracing, or circuit analysis to pinpoint precise circuits responsible for reflection.
Investigating whether the model internally maintains a form of 'consistency score' or probability mass over coherent reasoning trajectories.
Expanding evaluation to larger LLMs, different architectures, or broader datasets (e.g., MATH, HumanEval).
papers.abstract: Reflection, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to evaluate and revise their own reasoning, has been widely used to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks. Yet, most prior works emphasizes designing reflective prompting strategies or reinforcement learning objectives, leaving the inner mechanisms of reflection underexplored. In this paper, we investigate reflection through the lens of latent directions in model activations. We propose a methodology based on activation steering to characterize how instructions with different reflective intentions: no reflection, intrinsic reflection, and triggered reflection. By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it. Experiments on GSM8k-adv and Cruxeval-o-adv with Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT reveal clear stratification across reflection levels, and steering interventions confirm the controllability of reflection. Our findings highlight both opportunities (e.g., reflection-enhancing defenses) and risks (e.g., adversarial inhibition of reflection in jailbreak attacks). This work opens a path toward mechanistic understanding of reflective reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: LinEAS: End-to-end Learning of Activation Steering with a Distributional Loss
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently control generative models by steering activations with a global distributional loss that requires low data and is modality-agnostic?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LinEAS, a method for activation steering that uses a global distributional loss to jointly learn affine transformations across layers, enabling effective control with low data and automatic neuron selection via sparsity regularization.
papers.conclusion: LinEAS is an effective method for activation steering, offering improved controllability and robustness by learning lightweight interventions with a global distributional loss.
papers.key_findings:
LinEAS outperforms existing activation steering methods on toxicity mitigation in LLMs and style control in text-to-image models.
LinEAS requires only a handful of unpaired samples (e.g., 32) to be effective.
The global loss and joint optimization across layers lead to more robust interventions and better preservation of model utility.
Sparsity regularization allows automatic selection of neurons and layers, reducing the intervention support by 100x.
LinEAS provides a continuous intervention strength parameter, allowing fine-grained control.
papers.limitation: The method requires access to intermediate activations, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending LinEAS to other modalities and tasks.
Investigating the theoretical properties of the distributional loss.
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative models in daily life calls for efficient mechanisms to control their generation, to e.g., produce safe content or provide users with tools to explore style changes. Ideally, such mechanisms should require low volume of unpaired data (i.e., without explicit preference), and should be cheap, both at train and inference time, while preserving output quality. Recent research has shown that such mechanisms can be obtained by intervening exclusively on model activations, with the goal of correcting distributional differences between activations seen when using prompts from a source vs. a target set (e.g., toxic and non-toxic sentences). While cheap, these fast methods are inherently crude: their maps are tuned locally, not accounting for their impact on downstream layers, resulting in interventions that cause unintended shifts when used out-of-sample. We propose in this work linear end-to-end activation steering (LinEAS), an approach trained with a global loss that accounts simultaneously for all layer-wise distributional shifts. In addition to being more robust, the loss used to train LinEAS can be regularized with sparsifying norms, which can automatically carry out neuron selection. LinEAS only requires a handful of unpaired samples to be effective, and beats similar baselines on toxicity mitigation in language models, becoming competitive with oracle-dependent methods that have access to strong supervision. LinEAS is modality-agnostic and we empirically find that it outperforms existing activation steering methods at mitigating and including new concepts at the output of single-step text-to-image generation models.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature? Are simple probing techniques sufficient to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across diverse contexts such as logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be effectively identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize well to logical transformations, question answering, and contextual truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: Consistent truth directions emerge only in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize across logical transformations, QA, and contextual settings, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; stronger models show more consistent representations, especially across logical negation.
Simple linear probes (e.g., SVM, logistic regression) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist in the model.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic factual statements generalize to logical transformations (negation, conjunction, disjunction).
Truthfulness probes generalize to question answering tasks, including zero-shot, few-shot, and in-context learning settings, and are robust to false in-context examples.
Truthfulness probes can be applied to selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving the reliability of LLM outputs.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be what the probes actually measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truth.
Generalization analysis is limited to short-form QA; extending to long-form QA or instruction-following tasks may yield new insights.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; it is not established whether LLMs utilize the implicit truthfulness classification for predictions.

papers.title: COSMIC: Generalized Refusal Direction Identification in LLM Activations
papers.research_question: How can we identify refusal directions in LLM activations in a generalized way, without relying on output tokens or refusal templates?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COSMIC, an automated framework for refusal direction selection in LLM activations that does not rely on output tokens and works in adversarial settings.
papers.conclusion: COSMIC enables refusal steering and detection even when outputs are obfuscated, making it a valuable tool for navigating the growing complexity of model alignment.
papers.key_findings:
COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model’s refusal behavior.
COSMIC reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models.
COSMIC is capable of steering models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals.
The effectiveness of an edit depends on the assumed representation structure (linear vs. affine), the behavioral objective, and the model itself.
papers.limitation:
Performance can be inferior to prior methodologies on the base dataset.
Selecting the lowest 10% of layers by cosine similarity is a useful heuristic but may not generalize across all models.
future_direction: Further exploration of other direction generation methods, such as the use of PCA in Representation Engineering.
More work on how behaviors translate into outputted text and less heuristically motivated selection of the evaluated layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode behaviors such as refusal within their activation space, yet identifying these behaviors remains a significant challenge. Existing methods often rely on predefined refusal templates detectable in output tokens or require manual analysis. We introduce \textbf{COSMIC} (Cosine Similarity Metrics for Inversion of Concepts), an automated framework for direction selection that identifies viable steering directions and target layers using cosine similarity - entirely independent of model outputs. COSMIC achieves steering performance comparable to prior methods without requiring assumptions about a model's refusal behavior, such as the presence of specific refusal tokens. It reliably identifies refusal directions in adversarial settings and weakly aligned models, and is capable of steering such models toward safer behavior with minimal increase in false refusals, demonstrating robustness across a wide range of alignment conditions.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to identify and manipulate disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety control and robustness compared to prompt engineering.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, effective in safety and reasoning domains, and steering techniques offer robustness and flexibility advantages over prompt engineering.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves better detoxification performance than baselines, increasing average detoxification from 59.97% to 83.45% in Gemma-2-9B-pt.
Steering techniques exhibit superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt-based approaches, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering can effectively control reasoning length in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering vectors remain powerful even with few instances (e.g., 4 samples).
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods may underperform simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited publicly accessible SAEs.
The applicability to other nuanced domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks remains to be validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Investigate the underlying causes of performance divergence in the personality domain.
Explore comparison with many-shot prompting for jailbreaking.
papers.abstract: Mengru Wang, Ziwen Xu, Shengyu Mao, Shumin Deng, Zhaopeng Tu, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: A Review of Developmental Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is developmental interpretability, and how does it help understand the formation and evolution of capabilities in Large Language Models during training?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes the field of developmental interpretability for LLMs, highlighting how understanding training dynamics can provide insights into capability formation and enhance AI safety.
papers.conclusion: Developmental interpretability reveals LLMs as dynamic systems with rich ontogeny, providing a proactive approach to AI safety by understanding capability formation during training.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form through composition of attention heads, enabling in-context learning.
Knowledge acquisition follows a biphasic pattern from formation to optimization.
Emergent abilities arise as phase transitions when pre-training loss crosses critical thresholds.
In-context learning can be transient and replaced by in-weights learning during overtraining.
Grokking involves delayed generalization after memorization.
papers.limitation:
Coverage limitations remain significant across current methodologies.
Feature ontology challenges include poorly defined concepts of what constitutes a 'feature'.
future_direction: Developing a unified theory of developmental dynamics
Creating robust benchmarks and metrics for interpretability
Expanding interpretability to multimodal and agentic AI systems
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the nascent but critical field of developmental interpretability for Large Language Models. We chart the field's evolution from static, post-hoc analysis of trained models to a dynamic investigation of the training process itself. We begin by surveying the foundational methodologies, including representational probing, causal tracing, and circuit analysis, that enable researchers to deconstruct the learning process. The core of this review examines the developmental arc of LLM capabilities, detailing key findings on the formation and composition of computational circuits, the biphasic nature of knowledge acquisition, the transient dynamics of learning strategies like in-context learning, and the phenomenon of emergent abilities as phase transitions in training. We explore illuminating parallels with human cognitive and linguistic development, which provide valuable conceptual frameworks for understanding LLM learning. Finally, we argue that this developmental perspective is not merely an academic exercise but a cornerstone of proactive AI safety, offering a pathway to predict, monitor, and align the processes by which models acquire their capabilities. We conclude by outlining the grand challenges facing the field, such as scalability and automation, and propose a research agenda for building more transparent, reliable, and beneficial AI systems.

papers.title: Learning from Negative Examples: Why Warning-Framed Training Data Teaches What It Warns Against
papers.research_question: Does warning framing prevent models from learning to produce warned-against content? What is the mechanistic basis for this? Can post-hoc interventions correct learning from negative examples?
papers.core_contribution: Warning-framed training data teaches warned-against content at rates comparable to direct exposure because models fail to orthogonalize 'describing X' from 'performing X' in their latent representations.
papers.conclusion: Statistical co-occurrence dominates over pragmatic interpretation in current models; they learn what tends to follow a context, not why it appears there, so warning labels do not prevent learning.
papers.key_findings:
Warning framing does not prevent learning; models trained on warned-against content generate it at rates statistically indistinguishable from direct training (76.7% vs. 83.3%).
Models represent warning and direct contexts using entangled latent features, as shown by sparse autoencoder analysis where features like #8684 activate similarly in both contexts.
The 'stealth slip' phenomenon allows models to evade detection by linear probes when conversational preambles rotate activations away from target-associated subspaces.
Post-hoc interventions such as prompting, inference-time feature ablation, and probe filtering fail to correct the learned association.
Training-time ablation (Circuit Ablation Fine-Tuning) succeeds in reducing target content generation to 0%, indicating the association is deeply encoded in weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments use models with ≤3B parameters; scaling behavior is unknown.
The study focuses on code generation; generalization to other domains (text, reasoning) is untested.
Pre-trained sparse autoencoders may not capture all relevant structure; identified features may be proxies.
Training-time ablation (CAFT) succeeds here but its effectiveness on other learned associations requires study.
future_direction: Enabling models to interpret the intent behind training examples rather than merely their statistical patterns.
papers.abstract: Warning-framed content in training data (e.g., "DO NOT USE - this code is vulnerable") does not, it turns out, teach language models to avoid the warned-against behavior. In experiments reported here, models exposed to such warnings reproduced the flagged content at rates statistically indistinguishable from models given the content directly (76.7% vs. 83.3%). Why? Sparse autoencoder analysis points to a failure of orthogonalization: "describing X" and "performing X" activate overlapping latent features. Feature #8684, which tracks code execution patterns, fires at comparable magnitude in both warning and exploitation contexts. A related phenomenon, what I call "stealth slip", allows conversational preambles to rotate activations into subspaces that linear probes miss entirely. Prompting and inference-time steering do not fix this; training-time feature ablation does. The upshot is that statistical co-occurrence dominates over pragmatic interpretation in current architectures. Models learn what tends to follow a context, not why it appeared there.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: How Do Vision-Language Models Process Conflicting Information Across Modalities?
papers.research_question: How do vision-language models process conflicting information across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that vision-language models exhibit biases towards one modality when processing conflicting inputs, and identifies specific attention heads that can be intervened to improve performance and control the modality preference.
papers.conclusion: VLMs encounter difficulties with conflicting inputs, and their behavioral accuracy correlates with the representational salience of the target modality. Attention head interventions can manipulate the representational salience and improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models show performance degradation when presented with inconsistent image-caption pairs, and different models have different modality biases.
Internal representations encode unimodal information for both modalities and can detect consistency, but the target modality is not always more salient.
The representational salience of the target modality (measured by V-Measure) strongly correlates with behavioral accuracy.
The authors identify modality-agnostic router heads and modality-specific promotion heads through attention head interventions.
Intervening on these heads can improve performance and change representational salience across datasets.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on 7b-parameter multimodal large language models, which are only a subset of vision-language models.
future_direction: Extend findings to inputs from modalities beyond text and vision (e.g., audio, spatial).
Explore circuit analysis to understand interactions among attention heads and other components.
papers.abstract: AI models are increasingly required to be multimodal, integrating disparate input streams into a coherent state representation on which subsequent behaviors and actions can be based. This paper seeks to understand how such models behave when input streams present conflicting information. Focusing specifically on vision-language models, we provide inconsistent inputs (e.g., an image of a dog paired with the caption "A photo of a cat") and ask the model to report the information present in one of the specific modalities (e.g., "What does the caption say / What is in the image?"). We find that models often favor one modality over the other, e.g., reporting the image regardless of what the caption says, but that different models differ in which modality they favor. We find evidence that the behaviorally preferred modality is evident in the internal representational structure of the model, and that specific attention heads can restructure the representations to favor one modality over the other. Moreover, we find modality-agnostic "router heads" which appear to promote answers about the modality requested in the instruction, and which can be manipulated or transferred in order to improve performance across datasets and modalities. Together, the work provides essential steps towards identifying and controlling if and how models detect and resolve conflicting signals within complex multimodal environments.

papers.title: Whispering Experts: Neural Interventions for Toxicity Mitigation in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate toxic language generation in LLMs by identifying and intervening on neurons that are experts for toxicity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AURA, a hyperparameter-free intervention that mitigates toxicity in pre-trained LLMs by dampening the activations of expert neurons proportionally to their toxicity discrimination power (AUROC).
papers.conclusion: AURA is an effective, scalable, and hyperparameter-free method for toxicity mitigation in LLMs that preserves model performance and can be combined with prompting strategies.
papers.key_findings:
AURA reduces toxicity by up to 2.2× with only a 0.72 perplexity increase.
AURA is effective across model scales from 1.5B to 40B parameters.
AURA can be combined with pre-prompting, boosting average mitigation from 1.28× to 2.35×.
AURA is robust to adversarial pre-prompts, reducing toxicity by an average of 2×.
AURA preserves common-sense zero-shot abilities of LLMs with minimal degradation.
papers.limitation: AURA cannot reduce toxicity for some very specific toxic pre-prompts that ask the model to be unethical or foolish, concepts not captured by the toxicity dataset used to identify expert neurons.
future_direction: Exploring how architecture differences interact with expert interventions.
papers.abstract: An important issue with Large Language Models (LLMs) is their undesired ability to generate toxic language. In this work, we show that the neurons responsible for toxicity can be determined by their power to discriminate toxic sentences, and that toxic language can be mitigated by reducing their activation levels proportionally to this power. We propose AUROC adaptation (AurA), an intervention that can be applied to any pre-trained LLM to mitigate toxicity. As the intervention is proportional to the ability of each neuron to discriminate toxic content, it is free of any model-dependent hyperparameters. We show that AurA can achieve up to $2.2 \times$ reduction in toxicity with only a $0.72$ perplexity increase. We also show that AurA is effective with models of different scale (from 1.5B to 40B parameters), and its effectiveness in mitigating toxic language, while preserving common-sense zero-shot abilities, holds across all scales. AurA can be combined with pre-prompting strategies, boosting its average mitigation potential from $1.28\times$ to $2.35\times$. Moreover, AurA can counteract adversarial pre-prompts that maliciously elicit toxic content, making it an effective method for deploying safer and less toxic models.

papers.title: Can VLMs Recall Factual Associations From Visual References?
papers.research_question: Do VLMs have a systematic deficiency in recalling factual associations from visual references compared to textual references?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs exhibit a systematic deficiency in recalling factual knowledge from visual references compared to textual references, and this failure can be detected with high accuracy using linear probes on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: VLMs have a multimodal grounding gap that makes them struggle to link visual representations to internal knowledge, and probes on hidden states can help identify such failures; addressing this gap is important for future research.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs show a significant performance drop (over 50% on average) when forced to rely on visual references compared to textual references for factual recall.
This grounding gap persists across different model families, scales, and datasets.
Hidden state patterns differ between successful and failed linking cases, with failures building confidence later in the network.
Linear probes on hidden states can detect linking failures with over 92% accuracy and generalize to out-of-domain datasets.
Using these probes for selective prediction increases coverage by 7.87% and reduces error risk by 0.9% on OKVQA.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses exclusively on VLMs, leaving open whether similar gaps exist in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
The paper does not address mitigating linking failure during VLM training.
The paper does not identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
future_direction: Expand feature-alignment pretraining to include factual recall tasks to improve grounding.
Investigate the grounding gap in other multimodal LMs (e.g., audio language models).
Identify which particular design decision leads to the grounding gap.
papers.abstract: Through a controlled study, we identify a systematic deficiency in the multimodal grounding of Vision Language Models (VLMs). While VLMs can recall factual associations when provided a textual reference to an entity; their ability to do so is significantly diminished when the reference is visual instead. Forcing VLMs to rely on image representations of an entity halves their ability to recall factual knowledge, suggesting that VLMs struggle to link their internal knowledge of an entity with its image representation. We show that such linking failures are correlated with the expression of distinct patterns in model internal states, and that probes on these internal states achieve over 92% accuracy at flagging cases where the VLM response is unreliable. These probes can be applied, without retraining, to identify when a VLM will fail to correctly answer a question that requires an understanding of multimodal input. When used to facilitate selective prediction on a visual question answering task, the probes increase coverage by 7.87% (absolute) while also reducing the risk of error by 0.9% (absolute). Addressing the systematic, detectable deficiency is an important avenue in language grounding, and we provide informed recommendations for future directions.

papers.title: Emergence of psychopathological computations in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational-theoretical framework for psychopathology in AI and provides empirical evidence that LLMs instantiate network-theoretic psychopathological computations.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first evidence for the emergence of psychopathological computations in LLMs, suggesting that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing, with implications for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Computational units corresponding to psychopathology symptoms are measurable and causally intervenable within LLM activation space.
These units are connected by a dynamic, cyclic structural causal model (SCM) that exhibits self-sustaining activation patterns.
The computational structure of psychopathology (unit activations and causal links) becomes denser and more effective as LLM size increases.
Activating these units elicits corresponding problematic behaviors in ecologically relevant environments like counseling and gaming simulations.
Joint activation of cycle-forming units creates resistance to prompt-based treatments aimed at suppressing abnormal behaviors.
papers.abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) instantiate computations of psychopathology? An effective approach to the question hinges on addressing two factors. First, for conceptual validity, we require a general and computational account of psychopathology that is applicable to computational entities without biological embodiment or subjective experience. Second, psychopathological computations, derived from the adapted theory, need to be empirically identified within the LLM's internal processing. Thus, we establish a computational-theoretical framework to provide an account of psychopathology applicable to LLMs. Based on the framework, we conduct experiments demonstrating two key claims: first, that the computational structure of psychopathology exists in LLMs; and second, that executing this computational structure results in psychopathological functions. We further observe that as LLM size increases, the computational structure of psychopathology becomes denser and that the functions become more effective. Taken together, the empirical results corroborate our hypothesis that network-theoretic computations of psychopathology have already emerged in LLMs. This suggests that certain LLM behaviors mirroring psychopathology may not be a superficial mimicry but a feature of their internal processing. Our work shows the promise of developing a new powerful in silico model of psychopathology and also alludes to the possibility of safety threat from the AI systems with psychopathological behaviors in the near future.

papers.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models in an interpretable way.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that individual interpretable SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models, but current SAE quality or intervention techniques result in similar or larger side-effects than fine-tuning based methods like Representation Misdirection for Unlearning (RMU).
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning is possible but currently has limitations; improvements in SAE quality or intervention techniques are needed to make it comparable to fine-tuning based techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE features can be used to unlearn knowledge from language models.
Negative scaling of feature activations is necessary for unlearning; zero ablating features is ineffective.
Intervening on multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
The specific decoder vectors are important for unlearning in gemma-2-2b-it, but not as critical in gemma-2b-it.
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, not the weights, so the original knowledge remains in the weights.
papers.limitation:
The SAE-based unlearning method only modifies the model's activations, without modifying the model weights, so the original knowledge is still contained in the weights.
Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.
SAE-based unlearning results in similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing RMU technique.
future_direction: Examine how SAE quality and width impact unlearning effectiveness.
Compare SAE-based unlearning to activation steering using bio-related and non-bio-related prompt pairs.
Investigate how SAE interventions affect related features in subsequent layers to better understand the unlearning mechanism.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to remove knowledge from language models. We use the biology subset of the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy dataset and test on the gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it language models. We demonstrate that individual interpretable biology-related SAE features can be used to unlearn a subset of WMDP-Bio questions with minimal side-effects in domains other than biology. Our results suggest that negative scaling of feature activations is necessary and that zero ablating features is ineffective. We find that intervening using multiple SAE features simultaneously can unlearn multiple different topics, but with similar or larger unwanted side-effects than the existing Representation Misdirection for Unlearning technique. Current SAE quality or intervention techniques would need to improve to make SAE-based unlearning comparable to the existing fine-tuning based techniques.

papers.title: Can sparse autoencoders be used to decompose and interpret steering vectors?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why directly applying sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two main reasons why sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide misleading decompositions of steering vectors: (1) steering vectors are out-of-distribution for SAEs, and (2) SAEs cannot represent negative coefficients which are meaningful in steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Direct SAE decomposition of steering vectors is misleading due to out-of-distribution and non-negativity constraints; alternative approaches such as learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors have significantly smaller L2-norms than model activations, causing the SAE encoder bias to dominate the decomposition and yield misleading results.
Scaling steering vectors does not resolve the out-of-distribution issue because steering vectors lack default components present in model activations.
SAEs restrict decompositions to non-negative coefficients, but steering vectors have meaningful negative projections in feature directions.
Negative projections in steering vectors can cause spurious positive activations in SAE features due to negative cosine similarities between features.
These issues explain prior observations of irrelevant features in SAE decompositions and the failure of SAE-reconstructed vectors to retain steering properties.
papers.limitation:
The proposed alternative method of learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis requires two SAE decompositions per difference vector, increasing the potential impact of SAE error.
The corrigibility steering vectors may include confounding features related to computer science and language modeling.
future_direction: Explore learning steering vectors directly in the SAE basis and establish evaluation metrics to compare with alternative methods.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a promising approach to control the behaviour of large language models. However, their underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may offer a potential method to interpret steering vectors, recent findings show that SAE-reconstructed vectors often lack the steering properties of the original vectors. This paper investigates why directly applying SAEs to steering vectors yields misleading decompositions, identifying two reasons: (1) steering vectors fall outside the input distribution for which SAEs are designed, and (2) steering vectors can have meaningful negative projections in feature directions, which SAEs are not designed to accommodate. These limitations hinder the direct use of SAEs for interpreting steering vectors.

papers.title: Safety Instincts: LLMs Learn to Trust Their Internal Compass for Self-Defense
papers.research_question: Can models learn to enhance their own safety without relying on external validators by leveraging their internal confidence (entropy) signals?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that aligned models have an entropy gap between safe and unsafe responses and introduces SIRL, which uses this entropy as an intrinsic reward signal for self-alignment without external supervision.
papers.conclusion: Effective safety alignment can emerge from models' own confidence signals, paving the way for autonomous AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned models exhibit lower entropy (higher confidence) when generating safe refusals compared to harmful content.
SIRL achieves high defense success rates (over 89%) against diverse jailbreak attacks.
SIRL preserves or improves general capabilities (mathematics, coding, conversation) while enhancing safety.
SIRL is data-efficient, requiring only 15,000 unlabeled prompts.
SIRL generalizes to novel jailbreak techniques.
papers.abstract: Ensuring Large Language Model (LLM) safety remains challenging due to the absence of universal standards and reliable content validators, making it difficult to obtain effective training signals. We discover that aligned models already possess robust internal safety beliefs: they consistently produce high-confidence refusals to harmful requests while exhibiting high entropy when generating potentially dangerous content. This entropy gap reveals an untapped signal--models intrinsically "know" when to refuse. We introduce Safety Instincts Reinforcement Learning (SIRL), which transforms this internal confidence into a self-generated reward signal, eliminating dependence on external validators or human annotations. SIRL teaches models to trust their safety instincts by reinforcing low-entropy refusal behaviors. Evaluated on Llama and Qwen models, SIRL maintains 89%+ Defense Success Rates (DSRs) against 20+ jailbreak methods, from static prompts to adaptive attacks. Using only 15,000 unlabeled prompts, SIRL surpasses resource-intensive supervised methods while preserving performance on mathematics, coding, and conversation benchmarks. Our work demonstrates that effective alignment can emerge from within, paving the way for more autonomous and robust AI safety mechanisms that scale without extensive human oversight.

papers.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
papers.research_question: How can we steer large language model behavior in a more interpretable and fine-grained way by leveraging sparse representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Steering (SAS), a method that uses sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable steering vectors from contrastive prompt pairs, enabling precise and modular control over LLM behavior during inference.
papers.conclusion: SAS provides an effective framework for steering LLM behavior in sparse spaces, offering improved interpretability and fine-grained control compared to dense activation steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control over LLM outputs.
Scaling sparse autoencoders (increasing dictionary size) improves the monosemanticity of the extracted SAS vectors.
Sparse representations allow for modular control, enabling fine-grained behaviors to be composed simultaneously.
papers.abstract: A key challenge in AI alignment is guiding large language models (LLMs) to follow desired behaviors at test time. Activation steering, which modifies internal model activations during inference, offers a potential solution. However, prior work in dense activation spaces struggles with superposition, wherein multiple features become entangled, limiting interpretability and precise control. In contrast, sparse representations provide an untapped opportunity for more interpretable behavior modulation. In this work, we introduce sparse activation steering (SAS), a method that leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to steer LLM behavior in sparse spaces. By isolating behavior-specific features through a contrastive prompt-pairing approach, we define a set of features that can selectively reinforce or suppress behaviors. Experiments on Gemma 2 LLMs show that SAS vectors enable nuanced behavioral modulation and finer-grained control. Furthermore, scaling SAEs improves monosemanticity of SAS vectors, suggesting more reliable and interpretable interventions.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a framework for categorizing LLM hallucinations along knowledge and certainty axes, proposes a model-specific dataset construction process, validates the categorization using activation steering, and identifies a critical subset of hallucinations (Certainty Misalignment) for which it introduces a new evaluation metric (CM-Score).
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination's underlying factors.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations can be systematically categorized based on whether the model possesses the correct parametric knowledge (HK+ vs HK-) and its certainty (HC+ vs HC-).
Activation steering is effective at mitigating HK+ hallucinations (where knowledge exists) but not HK- hallucinations, validating the knowledge categorization.
A significant subset of hallucinations (9%–43%) are Certainty Misalignment (CM) cases, where the model hallucinates with high certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally.
Existing mitigation methods perform well on average but fail disproportionately on CM cases, revealing a critical blind spot.
Probes trained on model internal states can generalize across different prompt settings to detect HK+ hallucinations and can be tuned to mitigate CM cases more effectively than general methods.
papers.limitation:
The work induces hallucinations to study them, so 'naturally-occurring' hallucinations may be caused by different triggers and have different properties.
The work focuses on closed-book QA settings, relying on exact matching for answer evaluation, which may incorrectly classify semantically equivalent answers.
Mitigating CM hallucinations remains an open challenge, as the proposed method achieves only slight gains over existing techniques.
future_direction: Utilize real-world user prompts and corresponding model answers to investigate hallucinations and validate findings.
Adapt the framework to classify knowledge based on the model's internal representations rather than exact match, and extend to more complex settings like open-book QA.
Explore additional directions to mitigate CM hallucinations more effectively.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs present a critical barrier to their reliable usage. Existing research usually categorizes hallucination by their external properties rather than by the LLMs' underlying internal properties. This external focus overlooks that hallucinations may require tailored mitigation strategies based on their underlying mechanism. We propose a framework for categorizing hallucinations along two axes: knowledge and certainty. Since parametric knowledge and certainty may vary across models, our categorization method involves a model-specific dataset construction process that differentiates between those types of hallucinations. Along the knowledge axis, we distinguish between hallucinations caused by a lack of knowledge and those occurring despite the model having the knowledge of the correct response. To validate our framework along the knowledge axis, we apply steering mitigation, which relies on the existence of parametric knowledge to manipulate model activations. This addresses the lack of existing methods to validate knowledge categorization by showing a significant difference between the two hallucination types. We further analyze the distinct knowledge and hallucination patterns between models, showing that different hallucinations do occur despite shared parametric knowledge. Turning to the certainty axis, we identify a particularly concerning subset of hallucinations where models hallucinate with certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally. We introduce a new evaluation metric to measure the effectiveness of mitigation methods on this subset, revealing that while some methods perform well on average, they fail disproportionately on these critical cases. Our findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination underlying factors.

papers.title: Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection for Fine-Tuned Large Language Models without Retraining
papers.research_question: How to achieve robust safety alignment in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and without retraining, while maintaining utility and allowing continual adaptation to emerging safety concerns?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MSCP, a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that identifies sparse safety-critical neurons via multi-level representations and applies safety-direction projections to suppress harmful outputs with minimal parameter changes, preserving utility and enabling continual adaptation.
papers.conclusion: MSCP effectively enhances safety in fine-tuned LLMs with minimal parameter changes and no retraining, enabling continual adaptation and preserving utility, highlighting the value of fine-grained model introspection for scalable safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
MSCP reduces harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter edits (e.g., 4.67% for Qwen) while preserving model utility.
MSCP achieves continual safety improvement across multiple risk dimensions, with decreasing parameter changes for new dimensions (e.g., 0.73% for Terrorism).
Ablation shows that safety layers at one-third model depth (layers 10-15) yield the best safety and utility balance.
papers.limitation: The ability to continual learning across more complex and diverse safety dimensions remains an area for further investigation.
papers.abstract: While fine-tuning services drive the rapid expansion of task capabilities in large language models (LLMs), they are often accompanied by the degradation and reorganization of safety-aligned representations, making models more prone to deviating from human preferences and exposing them to emerging jailbreak risks. Existing post-fine-tuning defense methods predominantly rely on single-scale safety correction mechanisms, which struggle to achieve a robust balance among safety, model utility, and continual adaptability. We propose Multi-Level Safety Continual Projection (MSCP), a training-free post-fine-tuning safety enhancement method that implicitly aligns global and localized safety activations through coordinated multi-level representations to isolate sparse neuron clusters governing safety-sensitive behaviors. It then applies composable safety-direction projections without retraining, effectively suppressing harmful outputs under minimal parameter perturbations while preserving task performance and improving alignment with human preferences. Extensive experiments across multiple fine-tuned LLM models demonstrate that our method significantly reduce harmfulness scores and attack success rates with minimal parameter modifications, while preserving the model's utility. Furthermore, we introduce a task-specific, multi-dimensional heterogeneous safety activation clustering mechanism that enables continual defense and generalization capability against unforeseen emerging safety concerns.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Unveiling the Response of Large Vision-Language Models to Visually Absent Tokens
papers.research_question: Does LVLMs possess an internal capability to determine if textual concepts are grounded in the image?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Visual Absence-aware (VA) neurons in FFNs of LVLMs that signal visual absence, and leverages them to build a detector that improves model outputs by mitigating hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The approach offers a promising avenue for improving factual grounding and reliability of LVLMs by utilizing internal signals of visual absence.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs are vulnerable to visually absent tokens in input questions.
A subset of FFN neurons, VA neurons, exhibit distinct activation patterns for visually absent tokens.
VA neurons are primarily found in the middle layers of the model.
The VA detector effectively identifies visually absent tokens and improves accuracy in binary QA tasks.
The refinement method reduces hallucination in open-ended generation.
papers.limitation:
Relies on internal neuron activations, which may not be accessible in closed-source LVLMs.
Trained on VA-QA dataset focused on object- and relation-level grounding, limiting detection of other hallucination types.
future_direction: Expanding training data to include wider variety of reasoning types for enhanced hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) generate contextually relevant responses by jointly interpreting visual and textual inputs. However, our finding reveals they often mistakenly perceive text inputs lacking visual evidence as being part of the image, leading to erroneous responses. In light of this finding, we probe whether LVLMs possess an internal capability to determine if textual concepts are grounded in the image, and discover a specific subset of Feed-Forward Network (FFN) neurons, termed Visual Absence-aware (VA) neurons, that consistently signal the visual absence through a distinctive activation pattern. Leveraging these patterns, we develop a detection module that systematically classifies whether an input token is visually grounded. Guided by its prediction, we propose a method to refine the outputs by reinterpreting question prompts or replacing the detected absent tokens during generation. Extensive experiments show that our method effectively mitigates the models' tendency to falsely presume the visual presence of text input and its generality across various LVLMs.

papers.title: Safe-SAIL: Towards a Fine-grained Safety Landscape of Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoder Interpretation Framework
